Yeah. My back-of-a-napkin calculation came up with a big fat nope.

Example:

Average lifespan of ~7 decades

Average 20 U.S. serial killers emerge per year. Assume all are dead or in prison in exactly 10 years, and that they're on average 30 years old when they start (giving you 40 years to meet them).

This gives about 800 current or future serial killers available in the general population at any given time for you to meet.

US population ~325,000,000

New people met daily on average: 2

New people met per lifespan less early childhood: ~40,000

Odds that any particular person you meet is a current or future serial killer: 800 / 325,000,000 = .0000025 = .00025%.

Probability you will meet a current or future serial killer in your lifetime: ~9%.

Every time I had to make an assumption - several dozen times - I made the most generous, serial-killer-meeting-promoting assumption that I reasonably could. For example, I assume that you meet newborn babies at the same rate you meet 20-somethings and so on. I assume that serial killers meet strangers at the same rate as average people. Etc.

The most interesting thing I learned was the idea of free won't vs free will.

Essentially we don't have a choice in the actions we take, we have a temporary reflection on the actions we're going to take and veto decision against those actions.

For instance, you're hungry, you go to the fridge, you see the cheese sticks and burger meat and while you may have a craving for cheese, you veto that decision because you want to stick to your diet, and make burgers instead.

This willpower to veto these decisions is limited though, and each choice drains us of our ability to veto future choices. It's an effect known as ego depletion.

The idea is subtle, but it really makes sense, especially in the context of defining how you want to accomplish things.

Hi all,

I'd like to shamelessly promote a new tool I've written, RAFTools. I was a little annoyed at how RAFManager handled loading and extracting LoL's RAF files, specifically each patch being given its own folder made it hard to find files easily.

RAFTools will "mount" the patches in order, applying the changes on top of each other, in the right order so you essentially have a complete filesystem, same as what the game sees.

You can open a specific archive and "apply/add" a patch to it. Or you just simply open the entire LoL directory. Extraction of files/directories is fully supported (right-click on the file/folder -> Extract) Modification of archives isn't supported yet - the code is there, it's just very unstable in its current state.

This is still only an alpha version, and there are a few known bugs, but naturally there will be new ones cropping up. I would appreciate it if you posted back here if you find any. Actually, if you really feel like being nice, you can report them on the issue tracker.

For those seeing this from the /r/leagueoflegends subreddit, welcome!

EDIT: Code has been open-sourced.

Screenshot

DOWNLOAD:

https://github.com/vs49688/RAFTools

USAGE:

java -jar RAFTools-0.4.3-alpha.jar [-console]

Specifying -console will disable the GUI and attach to the currently-running terminal.

  • Not multi-threaded, like the GUI - Will wait for a command to be completed before allowing you to enter another.

KNOWN BUGS / BEHAVIOUR NOTES:

  • Malformed .raf/.raf.dat files will probably cause the program to throw an Exception.
  • The directory tree in the GUI is dynamically updated as the VFS is built, so it's best to wait until the console tells you that the file's been loaded before starting extraction.

CURRENT FEATURES:

  • Viewing/Extraction of RAF files
  • .inibin/.troybin decoder/viewer
  • Embedded .DDS viewer (textures)

I always wanted to learn reverse engineering games, but never know how to start. Got any tips?

Assuming you know basic programming (If you don't, try starting with Python):

  • First thing: Google. If you're trying to RE something, check Google first. Chances are someone's already done it. A lot of the code in RAFTools is based on information previously discovered by others.
  • Learn your DLLs and EXEs and how they work - if you know what's in them, you'll be able to rip stuff out of them more easily.
    • Here is a good place to start.
  • Learn about binary and text file formats and the difference between them.
  • For PC Games, learn x86 and x86_64 Assembly - unless the game is open source (why would you be RE'ing it then?), then it is essential to learn to read assembly (writing, not so much, but it helps). Why? Because EXEs contain machine code. Machine code can be mapped directly to assembly (which is a lot easier to read than straight binary).
  • Once you know all this, the basic algorithm is this:
    • Start the game in a debugger
    • Debug
    • ???
    • Profit!!!
  • And the most important thing: Enjoy it
    • RE'ing is hard and sometimes tedious work; unless you enjoy it (or are being paid exuberant amounts of money), you probably won't get far.
